rules.title: Application screening fee cap and refund rules (Civil Code § 1950.6)
rules.requirement: A landlord can charge a screening fee only up to its actual costs. The fee can never be more than $30 per applicant, adjusted each year for inflation since 1998 (Berkeley lists $68.96 for 2026). The landlord can't charge a fee if it knows no unit is or soon will be available. It must give you an itemized receipt, refund any part it doesn't use, and give you a copy of your credit report within 7 days. It must also either consider applications in the order received and charge only the applicants it actually considers, or refund the whole fee to every applicant it doesn't pick, within 7 days of choosing a tenant or 30 days after you applied, whichever comes first.
rules.key_value: $30 per applicant, CPI-adjusted annually from 1998 ($68.96 for 2026 per Berkeley)
rules.coverage_conditions: Owners of residential rental property in California and their agents who charge applicants a fee to screen an application. Guarantors and cosigners count as applicants. No building limits.
rules.exemptions: Does not override deposit and fee rules under federal or state housing assistance programs. Under the first-come process, no refund is owed to an applicant who was considered and denied for failing the landlord's written screening criteria.
rules.reason: All five candidates describe provisions of Civil Code § 1950.6 (the fee cap, receipt and credit-report rules, the ban when no unit is available, and the first-come-or-refund rule), so they were merged into one record. Effective date left null: the 2026-01-01 date in one candidate looks like an amendment or yearly adjustment date, not when the cap began.
